name: Writing a Critical Review
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: So You Want to Fact-Check a Headline: Writing the Critical Review
lesson.summary: A critical review is a structured, repeatable piece of writing, not a gut reaction, that pins down the exact claim, weighs it against the extraordinary claims rule, traces it back past the press release to its source, and states a calibrated verdict instead of a simple yes or no.
lesson.body:
Reading skeptically and writing a critical review are two different skills, and this course has spent most of its time on the first one. Reading skeptically happens in your own head, you notice a red flag, you feel less certain, you move on. Writing a critical review is a public act, it has to withstand someone else pushing back on it, and that requires turning a private hunch into a structured argument with an actual chain of reasoning someone else can check.

Take a composite, deliberately generic example, the kind of headline that recurs with different technology names inserted: "New Quantum Chip Solves in Minutes a Problem That Would Take the World's Fastest Supercomputer Thousands of Years." The first job of a critical review is not to praise or debunk that sentence, it is to pin down exactly what is being claimed, because "solves a problem" is doing an enormous amount of unstated work. Solves which specific problem, under which specific conditions, compared against which specific classical algorithm, run on which specific classical hardware. A headline claim usually compresses several of these into one triumphant sentence, and a critical review's first paragraph should decompress it back into the specific, checkable version.

Once the claim is stated precisely, the extraordinary claims rule tells you how much evidence it needs before you believe it. A claim that a research team achieved a specific speedup on one narrowly defined, deliberately chosen problem is a meaningfully more ordinary claim than a claim that the result generalizes to problems people actually care about, and those two versions require very different amounts of evidence. The review's job is to state which version is actually being made in the source material, not the more dramatic version the headline implies, and then to ask what would count as extraordinary evidence for that specific version: independent replication, a named and defensible classical baseline, published methodology someone else could run.

Finding that evidence means going past the headline entirely, which is where the science journalism problems chapter becomes a practical research step rather than background knowledge. A rigorous review traces the story back to its origin: was this covered under an embargo that forced every outlet to publish from the same press kit at the same moment, does the university or company communications office have its own framing baked in before a single journalist touched it, and does the underlying paper or technical report say something more hedged than the headline built on top of it. Often the honest, careful version of the claim is sitting in the paper's own limitations section, several paragraphs past where most coverage stopped reading.

The last step is applying the risk assessment framework to the review's own conclusion, not just to the original claim. A critical review should say plainly how much this would matter if the claim holds up and how much it would matter if it does not, because a review that spends all its energy debunking a claim with low real world stakes is not more rigorous than one that engages a high stakes claim carefully, it is just aimed at a smaller target. The finished review states three things clearly: the precise claim being made, what evidence would be needed to justify believing it and whether that evidence currently exists, and a calibrated verdict, not a simple confirmed or debunked, but something like "the narrow technical result is plausible and appears real, the generalization implied by the headline is not yet supported." That is a harder sentence to write than a verdict in either direction, and it is the one an honest review actually owes its reader.
